title: Overnight production, rest and a disputed quality deadline
narrative:
This is an authored supply-chain review file concerning a fictional small-parts factory.

A buyer's reviewer receives a complaint from an adult machine operator after a product launch. Production ran late on several nights because a batch failed quality inspection. The factory's written policy says overtime is voluntary, and a manager points to signed overtime slips. The worker acknowledges signing those slips but asks the reviewer to examine what happened when they requested rest rather than treating a signature as the whole answer.

The attendance system shows three consecutive shifts ending after midnight. It also shows late starts on two following days, although one late start may reflect a missing clock entry rather than time away from work. The worker kept handwritten notes of sleep and travel times. A payroll clerk has offered to reconcile them with machine logs. The operator wants that comparison made before anyone states a precise total of unpaid hours.

The operator lives in an off-site dormitory and holds their own identity document. A dormitory access card stops working after the ordinary evening entry time, but a staffed entrance remains open. The worker used that entrance after one late shift. A photograph of the electronic lock therefore provides limited evidence about actual movement. The complaint instead focuses on the employer's response to refusal and the rest available between duties.

A photograph also shows a portable fan near adhesive containers. The worker reports an unpleasant smell; the manager says the containers were closed and the room's extraction system was operating. No air measurement or maintenance record is supplied. That disagreement warrants a specific safety question, while the photograph does not establish exposure levels or a medical diagnosis.

The operator generally likes the skilled work and wants a predictable schedule rather than an immediate job change. A newer colleague depends on the operator for machine setup, creating an additional feeling of responsibility. The reviewer should consider that pressure without assuming that helping a colleague is always involuntary. The worker has requested a meeting away from supervisors and has not agreed to a named allegation in the buyer's report.

[MA-R1] Worker account: "When I refused another overnight shift, the supervisor said I would lose the pay already earned and my next month's shifts. I worked because of that warning."

[MA-R2] Supplied scheduling reply: "Your requested recovery day is cancelled. You must report again after four hours away from the factory." The worker's diary records that the same pattern occurred on three nights.

[MA-R3] Access note: "I hold my original identity document and used the staffed dormitory entrance after work."

What should the interview establish about working time and genuine refusal, and what immediate practical protections are appropriate? Separate substantiated statements from the ventilation and time-record uncertainties. Explain how the worker's priorities should affect any contact with factory management.
